# Paint

> A local-first sketchpad PWA: draw a concept on a canvas, switch extra tools on
> when you need them, and keep every drawing on your device — with optional
> Dropbox or Google Drive sync.

Paint is a small, installable web app for sketching the kind of diagram you draw
to explain something: boxes, arrows, a circled bit, a scribble. Drawings are
vector strokes stored as JSON in your browser; nothing is uploaded unless you
connect a storage backend yourself.

## What it does

- Draw with a pen, a graphite pencil, an eraser, a watercolour brush, an
  airbrush, a paint bucket (and the gradient behind it, which fills the same
  area with a ramp of its own colours), the shapes, a selection marquee, a text
  tool and a colour dropper, plus a hand tool that drags the page around — the
  toolbar out of the box.
- Set every tool in the sizes it is really made in. A page pixel is one dot of
  an iPhone's screen, so widths are millimetres you can measure on the glass at
  1:1: the pencil offers the
  four leads a mechanical pencil takes, the round brush a #2 through a one-inch
  flat, type is set in points, and each tool's slider spends its middle four
  tenths on the range that tool is genuinely manufactured in.
- Reach for a tool the way its medium is actually used: every tool ships with a
  row of presets — the pencil as Sketch, Construction, Shading and Detail, the
  watercolour brush as a wash, wet-in-wet, a glaze and a dry brush, the
  calligraphy pen as an italic, foundational or uncial hand — and each chip sets
  a width and every dial at once, showing the mark it makes.
- Paint a wash with either of two watercolour engines, switched in Settings →
  Tools: the fast stroke model the app ships with, or a pigment simulation that
  puts water and colour on the paper a step at a time and lets the mark be
  whatever dries — blooms, backruns, a frayed wet edge, granulation that rolls
  into the paper's valleys. Both read the same dials and the same paper; a
  browser that cannot run the simulation paints with the first one instead.
- Choose what the page is made of when the drawing is made, alongside its size:
  a solid digital sheet, four papers (hot-pressed, cold-pressed, rough,
  cartridge) or primed cotton duck. The sheet stays with the drawing and cannot
  be swapped afterwards, because a mark is painted into the sheet it was made
  on. Its grain is painted under the marks, and how wet a tool is times how
  thirsty the sheet is decides whether a mark covers what it is over or mixes
  into it, how far its water runs past the nib, and how much of an ink line it
  crosses it drags out into the wash. Wet mixing is scoped to one layer.
- Save a tool you have set up under a name — "my sketching pencil" — and get
  its width and every dial back in one press.
- Draw eleven shapes from one toolbar button: rectangle, ellipse, line, arrow,
  rounded rectangle, triangle, diamond, pentagon, hexagon, star and double
  arrow. Press the button a second time for the family and the fill toggle.
- Pick marks up again with the selection tools: draw a box, an oval or a
  freehand lasso over what you drew, or trace the contours of what is already
  painted — four gestures behind one button, pressed a second time to choose.
  Move what you caught with the hand, and copy, cut or delete it with the
  keyboard, a right-click or a long press. Ctrl/Cmd+V pastes marks, a picture or words back
  into the drawing — words open the caption box so the typeface and size are
  yours to set first.
- Press the eraser a second time for the rubber behind it: it lifts pencil and
  crayon the way a real one does — a little at a time, never all of it, and
  never the ink drawn over them.
- Switch more tools on in Settings → Tools (a round and a flat bristle brush,
  marker, highlighter, crayon, calligraphy pen), and put the rows in the order
  you want
  the toolbar in. Every tool is a plugin behind one interface, so the list grows
  without the app changing shape.
- Type on the page: the text tool opens a caret where you tap, in four
  typefaces, five type sizes, bold and italic. Drag the caption box to reposition
  it before you keep it.
- Pick colour and stroke width from two buttons: a palette with a free colour
  mixer that remembers what you mix, and a nib picker with your own widths. Every
  width is shown as a real press with the tool in your hand — the mark it would
  leave, on your page, in your ink — rather than as a dot. The width is
  remembered per tool, and each tool opens at a width of its own. Widths read in
  millimetres of page, from a technical pen's 0.5 to a decorator's 200.
- Tune the tool in your hand under the nib picker's Advanced fold — how charged
  the head is, its hair gauge, how far it has splayed and how far the paper
  bleeds for the paintbrush, flow for the airbrush, pressure for the crayon, the
  lead's grade for the pencil, the chisel of a felt tip for the marker and the
  highlighter, the nib's angle for the calligraphy pen, strength for the eraser,
  pressure for the rubber, a feathered edge for the paint bucket and the
  gradient, how much page one press of the dropper reads, opacity for most of
  the rest. Each tool keeps its own settings — including the inks a tool mixes
  for itself, like the gradient's two ends and its optional middle — and a mark
  remembers what it was drawn with. On a desktop the pointer is drawn as the nib
  itself: a circle the size of the mark, at the page's own scale.
- Start a drawing from an empty page, an image file, or an image on the
  clipboard. An empty one asks its canvas size up front — this screen, Full HD,
  4K, A4 or a size you type, drawn to one shared scale so they can be compared
  at a glance.
- Resize, flip (a quarter turn either way) and mirror a whole drawing from the
  right-hand panel; resizing can scale the drawing or change only the sheet,
  which is how a page is cropped or given more room. The resize dialog draws the
  new page over the old one and lets it be pulled by its corners, crop-tool
  style, with a latch that keeps the proportions. The same panel's bin starts
  the drawing over — every mark, every layer and the page colour.
- Blur the whole page or scatter grain over it from the right-hand panel's
  Filters section, with the amount, the speck size and coloured-or-grey grain set
  in the filter's own dialog. A filter is held on the drawing as a couple of
  numbers and composited when the page is painted — no mark is rasterised, so it
  is one undo step, it travels with the document, and switching it off gives the
  drawing back untouched. Downloads carry it: the raster formats through the same
  painting the screen does, an SVG as filter primitives.
- Draw on a page bigger than the window: the canvas is a window onto it, with
  pinch-to-zoom, two-finger panning, and one-finger panning under the hand.
- Stack a drawing into layers: swipe in from the right edge of the canvas (or
  use the header button) for a panel that adds, selects, shows, hides, locks,
  reorders and deletes them, each row previewing the marks on that layer. Every
  drawing starts with a locked Background layer — which carries the page colour,
  stays at the bottom of the stack and takes nothing underneath it, and is
  switched off on a page made with no colour — and one layer above it. New marks land on the selected layer; a hidden layer leaves the
  screen and every export, and a transparent export leaves the Background out
  entirely.
- Keep several drawings, group them into folders, star the ones you return to,
  and archive the rest instead of deleting them.
- Tidy the sidebar with the gesture at hand: on touch, swipe a row right to
  archive it or left to bare a Delete button, and hold it to pick it up and drag
  it onto a folder, out to the top level, onto another sketchbook, or onto the
  archive — every target outlines itself as the row lifts. On a desktop the same
  actions live behind a right-click menu, and rows drag with the mouse.
- Keep several namespaces (separate sketchbooks), each with its own document,
  and move a drawing (or a whole folder, drawings and all) between them by
  dragging it onto another sketchbook's row.
- Drop an image file onto the canvas to add it to a drawing — move and scale it
  before settling it, and the page grows if the picture is bigger than the sheet
  — or onto the drawings list to start a new drawing named after the file.
- Undo and redo every mark; download a page as PNG, JPG or SVG, copy it to the
  clipboard, or export the whole document as JSON. Settings → Download chooses
  which types the menu offers, whether a file covers the whole page or crops to
  the marks, and whether the background is kept or transparent. A page made with
  no colour of its own downloads transparent as PNG or SVG whatever that setting
  says; JPG, which has no transparency, is given the colour the sheet would have
  had.
- Save a whole drawing as a `.pct` paint file and open it again exactly as it
  was. It is a zip holding one transparent PNG per layer plus a readable
  `manifest.json` — so other tools can read the layers — and the vector marks
  in `vectors.json` alongside, which is what makes reopening it lossless rather
  than a flatten. Open one from New image → Load, or by dropping it there.
- Work offline: it is an installable PWA with a precaching service worker.
- Optionally sync to a local folder, Dropbox, or Google Drive, with optional
  end-to-end encryption of the synced file.
- Press the header's disk button (or Ctrl/Cmd+S) to file the rendered layers out
  to that backend as browsable PNGs under `drawings/<name>-<tag>/`. Only that
  half of a save is manual: the marks push themselves on every settled edit, as
  they always have. A layer whose pixels have not changed costs nothing on the
  next press, because each layer's file name carries a hash of its content.
